ref: DAR — Revelation ch. 5: The Heavenly Sanctuary (continued)
title: The Heavenly Sanctuary (continued)
voicePrompt: Explain in your own words Smith's account of the sealed book scene: who sits on the throne and what the book contains, why no being could open it and why John wept, how Christ as the slain Lamb prevailed to open it, and what the song of the redeemed and the final clean-universe anthem reveal.

questions.stem: According to Smith, who is meant by "him that sat on the throne" who holds the book, and what does the book contain?
options: Christ, holding a record of every person's sins
The Father, holding a revelation of scenes to transpire in the history of the church to the end of time
A strong angel, holding the law of God
The Holy Spirit, holding the names written in the book of life
questions.explanation: Smith says "him that sat on the throne" evidently means the Father, since the Son is afterward introduced as the slain Lamb; and the book contained a revelation of scenes that were to transpire in the history of the church to the end of time.

questions.stem: How does Smith describe the form of the "book" John saw, and what point does he draw from "written within and on the back side"?
options: It was a bound codex of leaves, written on every page
It was a roll of parchment; following Grotius and others, Smith removes the comma so it reads "written within, and on the back sealed"
It was a stone tablet engraved on both faces
It was a scroll written only by the angel who proclaimed the challenge
questions.explanation: Smith explains ancient books were rolled strips of parchment, not bound leaves, and that the long rolls were seldom written on more than the inward side; citing the Cottage Bible (Grotius, Lowman, Fuller), he removes the comma so the text reads "written within, and on the back (or outside) sealed."

questions.stem: What does Smith conclude from the fact that "no man in heaven" (Greek oudeis) was found able to open the book?
options: That the book was never meant to be opened by anyone
That only humans, not angels, were challenged to open it
That the word means not merely no man but no being, proving the faculties of angels are limited like man's in penetrating the future
That the angels refused out of reverence rather than inability
questions.explanation: Smith stresses that oudeis means not merely no man but no one, no being in heaven, and asks whether this is not proof that the faculties of angels are limited, like those of man, in respect to penetrating the future and disclosing what is to come.

questions.stem: Why, according to Smith, did John weep much, and what changed his weeping?
options: He wept from joy at seeing the throne, and an angel told him to be silent
He wept fearing the counsels of God for His people would never be disclosed, until an elder pointed him to the Lion of Juda who had prevailed
He wept over his own sins, and the Lamb forgave him
He wept because the seals were already broken, until they were restored
questions.explanation: Smith says John feared the counsels of God concerning His people would never be disclosed and so wept much; then one of the elders told him, "Weep not; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda... hath prevailed to open the book."

questions.stem: What does Smith say the word "prevailed" (the Lamb "hath prevailed" to open the book) indicates?
options: That Christ persuaded the Father to let Him open it
That the right to open the book was acquired by a victory gained in a previous conflict — Christ's death, resurrection, and triumph over the grave
That the Lamb out-argued the strong angel who issued the challenge
That prevailing simply means Christ was the most worthy by birthright as David's son
questions.explanation: Smith writes that "hath prevailed" indicates the right to open the book was acquired by a victory gained in a previous conflict: Christ bore the agonies of the cross, rose a victor over death and the grave, made redemption sure, and triumphed.

questions.stem: How does Smith interpret the redeemed ones (the four living creatures and elders) holding golden vials of odors, and their calling themselves kings and priests?
options: As angels performing worship distinct from the redeemed church
As assistants of Christ in His priestly work, offering incense (the prayers of saints) as the high priest's assistants did in the typical service
As prophets recording the prayers of the saints for later judgment
As a purely figurative image with no real beings behind it
questions.explanation: Smith says the vials of odors (incense), which are the prayers of saints, mark a work of ministry pertaining to priests; recalling the high priest's many assistants in the typical service, he concludes these redeemed ones are the assistants of our great High Priest above, for which purpose they were redeemed.

questions.stem: Smith argues the "new song" of verse 9 is sung by redeemed beings rather than angels. What is the song's anticipation in "we shall reign on the earth"?
options: That they already rule the nations from heaven in the present age
That they look forward to a still higher state, after redemption is completed, when the whole redeemed family will reign on the earth, their promised and eternal inheritance
That they will reign in heaven forever and never return to earth
That the earth will be ruled by the angels while the saints remain in heaven
questions.explanation: Smith says their song contemplates a still higher state — when redemption is completed and they, with the whole redeemed family of every age, shall reign on the earth, which is the promised inheritance and the final, eternal residence of the saints.

questions.stem: How does Smith explain the universal anthem of verse 13, where "every creature" blesses God and the Lamb?
options: It describes the present worship of the church on earth
It is thrown in out of chronological order, anticipating the time after redemption is finished, the wicked destroyed, and the universe cleansed of sin and sinners
It refers to the worship offered before sin entered the world
It proves that even the lost will one day praise God from a place of eternal torment
questions.explanation: Smith says verse 13 is a declaration thrown in out of chronological order, anticipating the time when redemption is finished; since no point in the past or present fits (cursings, not blessings, rise from the apostate race), the scene belongs to a clean universe after sin and sinners are destroyed by fire — leaving no room for an eternal receptacle of fire and torment.
